scripts.name: Brahmi
scripts.subtitle: Goykanadi / Kandavi
scripts.summary: The ancestor script of the region. Early Brahmi and archaic Dravidian Brahmi inscriptions appear in Goa and the Konkan from the 2nd century BC. Its Kadamba-lineage descendant, Goykanadi (also called Kandavi), was Goa's own indigenous script for Konkani, used for commerce and administration until it was largely destroyed under Portuguese rule.

communities.name: Trading Saraswat families
communities.note: Used Goykanadi for commercial accounts and records

communities.name: Daivajna families
communities.note: Kept mercantile ledgers in Goykanadi alongside Modi

catalysts.label: 2nd century BC
catalysts.text: Earliest Brahmi and archaic Dravidian Brahmi inscriptions appear across Goa and the Konkan coast.

catalysts.label: 2nd century AD
catalysts.text: First known Konkani inscription, at Arvalem, Goa: śacipurācē śirasi.

catalysts.label: c. 960 CE
catalysts.text: Kadamba dynasty rises; Goykanadi (Kandavi) script develops from the Kadamba Brahmi lineage.

catalysts.label: 15th century
catalysts.text: Earliest surviving Goykanadi document: a petition by Ravala Śeṭī.

catalysts.label: 24 Nov 1548
catalysts.text: Letter of João Afonso de Albuquerque documents Portuguese destruction of local-script manuscripts — the decisive blow against Goykanadi and other indigenous Goan scripts.

catalysts.label: 17th century
catalysts.text: Goykanadi loses popularity; Inquisition-era burnings destroy much of the remaining record.

scripts.contemporary: Purely historical and epigraphic today. No living writing community or speaker base. Scholarly recovery includes Gajanana Ghantkar's 1993 History of Goa through Goykanadi Script, and a Unicode encoding proposal has been raised for the script.

scripts.name: Modi
scripts.subtitle: Marathi administrative cursive
scripts.peakLabel: Shivaji era to end of Peshwa rule (c. 1600 – 1818)
scripts.summary: Primarily a Marathi administrative script, Modi was 'sometimes' used for Konkani too. Its cursive form suited fast record-keeping and it flourished under Maratha state scribes (the Chitnisi tradition) through the Shivaji and Peshwa administrations, and was retained by Portuguese Goa's administration for Maratha-facing correspondence.

communities.name: Trading Saraswat & Daivajna families
communities.note: Used Modi alongside Goykanadi for accounts

communities.name: Maratha state scribes
communities.note: Chitnisi tradition under Shivaji and the Peshwas

catalysts.label: 17th century
catalysts.text: Modi-Marathi officially used in Goa under Maratha/Bhonsle presence; Portuguese administration retains Modi translators.
End of Peshwa rule removes Modi's principal state sponsor.
Indian independence accelerates abandonment of Modi in favor of Devanagari for Marathi and Konkani alike.
Grassroots Modi revival movement begins in Pune.

catalysts.label: 22 Nov 2021
catalysts.text: One-month Modi-Marathi course launched at Sant Sohirobanath Government College, Pernem, Goa.

scripts.contemporary: Described as 'almost extinct' in Goa, with only two experts in the state. The Goa Archives holds land and temple records in Modi and mounted a 2022 exhibition of 16th–17th century Modi-Marathi documents. A Pune-based revival movement reported 400+ students by 2025 — but no Konkani-specific Modi publishing exists today.

scripts.name: Devanagari
scripts.subtitle: Nagari — the official script
scripts.summary: Nagari use for Konkani traces back to a disputed 10th-century Shravanabelagola inscription and firmer 12th–17th century records. Krishnadas Shama's 16th-century Konkani Ramayana and Mahabharata survive in Nagari copies. After decades of Portuguese suppression created a script vacuum, the 20th-century 'eki' (unity) movement led by Shenoi Goembab built the modern Devanagari standard, which the Sahitya Akademi and the Government of Goa later enshrined as official.

communities.name: Goud Saraswat Brahmins
communities.note: Principal carriers of the Nagari literary tradition

catalysts.label: 981 AD (disputed)
catalysts.text: Shravanabelagola inscription — attributed to Konkani by some scholars (Kulkarni, Pereira), though many linguists read it as Old Marathi.
Mahavali/Aparaditya II inscription — earliest inscription with lines read as Devanagari Konkani.

catalysts.label: 1520s
catalysts.text: Krishnadas Shama composes a Konkani Ramayana and Mahabharata; surviving copies are in Nagari.

catalysts.label: 27 Jun 1684
catalysts.text: Portuguese viceroy Dom Francisco de Tavora decrees a ban on Konkani, urged by Franciscans — confirmed by the king in 1687, tightened through 1745 and 1759, and not lifted until 1910.
William Carey's Devanagari Konkani New Testament — first complete Konkani book in Nagari.
Shenoi Goembab publishes his first Nagari book, launching the 'eki' (unity) movement for a standard Konkani.

catalysts.label: 8 Jul 1939
catalysts.text: All India Konkani Parishad, Kumta: Mahdav Shanbague proposes Devanagari as the sole official Konkani script.

catalysts.label: Apr 1962
catalysts.text: Jha Committee recommends Konkani as medium of instruction, in Nagari script if adopted.
Government of Kerala recognizes Konkani with Devanagari.

catalysts.label: 22 Aug 1970
catalysts.text: Goa CM Bandodkar declares Konkani in Devanagari official alongside Marathi.

catalysts.label: 26 Feb 1975
catalysts.text: Sahitya Akademi recognizes Konkani (in Devanagari) as an independent literary language.
Sahitya Akademi's Konkani Advisory Board unanimously recommends Nagari as the sole script.

catalysts.label: 4 Feb 1987
catalysts.text: Goa's Official Language Act passed: Konkani in Devanagari becomes the state's official language.
Konkani (Devanagari) added to the Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution.

scripts.contemporary: Devanagari is Konkani's sole officially recognized script — under Goa's 1987 Act and by the Government of India and Sahitya Akademi (reaffirmed 2024). Yet its position in education is fragile: Konkani-medium enrollment in Goa is just 8.8% of Class I–IV students (7,869 of 88,800), with ~300 government primary schools closed over a decade. In Kerala, the community deliberately switched from Malayalam to Nagari about 50 years ago.

sources.label: Navhind Times, 'Konkani: the script and the reality'

scripts.name: Roman
scripts.subtitle: Romi Konkani
scripts.summary: Konkani's oldest continuously preserved literary tradition. Introduced through Jesuit missionary printing — Asia's first printing press was set up in Goa in 1556 — Roman-script Konkani dominated the language's literature until Goa's 1961 liberation. It remains the vehicle of Goan Catholic liturgy, tiatr (musical theatre), and a still-active weekly press, but was excluded from official status by the 1987 Act.

communities.name: Goan Catholics / Goan Christians
communities.note: 25.10% of Goa's 2011 population; used in liturgy, tiatr, and print

communities.name: Mangalorean Catholics
communities.note: Roman-script literary presence in coastal Karnataka

catalysts.text: First Jesuit printing press in Asia established in Goa, seeding Roman-script Konkani literature.
Thomas Stephens publishes Doutrina Christam in Roman-script Konkani.
Thomas Stephens' Arte da Lingoa Canarim — foundational Konkani grammar in Roman script.
Fr Eduardo Bruno de Souza launches Udentechem Salok, first Konkani periodical, plus the first Konkani novel, Kristanv Ghorabo.

catalysts.label: 4 Jan 1933
catalysts.text: Vauraddeancho Ixtt weekly begins publication — still running, ~15,000 circulation, read in 50+ countries online.
Goa's Liberation from Portuguese rule — Roman script's dominant literary period ends as Devanagari gains ground.
Sahitya Akademi's single-script recognition excludes Roman-script writers from national awards despite the tradition's 1556 heritage.

catalysts.label: 4 Feb 1987
catalysts.text: Official Language Act omits Roman script — called a 'great betrayal' by Romi advocates.
Goa ordinance permits Roman script for some official communication, after a Bombay High Court PIL.

catalysts.label: 4 Feb 2024
catalysts.text: Global Romi Lipi Abhiyan holds symbolic protest on Official Language Day at Azad Maidan, Panjim.

scripts.contemporary: Roman-script Konkani has ~500,000 users. It receives partial institutional support — the Goa Konkani Akademi awards books in both Roman and Nagari, and the Dalgado Konknni Academy publishes exclusively in Roman script — but of 10 seats on the Sahitya Akademi's Konkani Advisory Board, only 1 traditionally represents Roman script. Tiatr (Goan musical theatre) produces roughly 300 shows a year, almost entirely in Romi Konkani. Active 2024–2025 campaigns continue to demand official recognition.

sources.label: Konkani in the Roman script, Wikipedia
Herald Goa, Global Romi Lipi Abhiyan

scripts.name: Kannada
scripts.subtitle: Coastal Karnataka's majority script
scripts.statusLabel: Majority script for Konkani in Karnataka today
scripts.summary: Kannada was the Kadamba court language from c. 960–1310, and Kannada-script Konkani writing dates at least to a 1538 signature. Goan migrant families who resettled in Karnataka after 1540 initially kept Nagari, but over generations lost contact with it and assimilated to the locally literate Kannada script — a shift documented in Fr Maffei's 1883 Konkani grammar and dictionary.

catalysts.label: c. 960–1310
catalysts.text: Kadambas rule Goa and coastal Karnataka with Kannada as court language.
Earliest known Kannada-script Konkani signature, by the first knighted Goan.

catalysts.label: post-1540
catalysts.text: Goan migrant families settle in Karnataka following Portuguese-era displacement, initially retaining Nagari.

catalysts.label: 18th–19th c.
catalysts.text: Later migrant generations lose contact with Nagari over 'a century or two' and shift to the locally literate Kannada script.
Fr A. F. X. Maffei's Konkani grammar and dictionary record that 'the Kanarese alphabet is now generally used'.
Karnataka introduces Konkani as optional third language (Kannada or Devanagari script) in Dakshina Kannada, Udupi and Uttara Kannada.

catalysts.label: Sep 2024
catalysts.text: Global Konknni Forum and Mandd Sobhann protest Sahitya Akademi's reaffirmed Devanagari-only policy at Mangaluru symposium.

scripts.contemporary: The majority practice among Konkani speakers in Karnataka. A Karnataka Konkani Sahitya Academy consultation found 44 of 67 respondents preferred Kannada script versus 19 for Devanagari and 2 for Roman; 88% of students, teachers and parents across 102 surveyed schools endorsed Kannada. Roughly 40 Kannada-script Konkani books were published in a single recent year (2004). 15% of Dakshina Kannada district's population speaks Konkani.

sources.label: The Hindu, Konkani academics in Karnataka
Navhind Times, 'Konkani: the script and the reality'

regions.note: Majority script; 15% of Dakshina Kannada speaks Konkani

scripts.name: Malayalam
scripts.subtitle: Kerala's residual Konkani script
scripts.statusLabel: Residual — largely superseded by Devanagari since the 1970s
scripts.summary: Konkani migrants who settled in Kerala initially wrote in Nagari — still evident in a 1675 testimonial — but later generations adopted the locally dominant Malayalam script as literacy assimilated to their new environment. About 50 years ago the community made a deliberate, organized reversal back to Devanagari, though pockets of Malayalam-script publishing persist.

communities.name: Kudumbis
communities.note: Concentrated in Cochin/Ernakulam and Alappuzha; publish the Marg Deepam monthly

communities.name: Gaud Saraswats, Vaishya Vani, Daivajna groups
communities.note: Bilingual in Malayalam, across Kochi, Alappuzha, Kollam, Kottayam

catalysts.text: Hortus Malabaricus testimonial by Cochin pandits shows Nagari still in active use among Kerala's Konkani community.

catalysts.label: 18th–19th c.
catalysts.text: Later generations assimilate to Malayalam literacy, gradually adopting the Malayalam script for Konkani.
Government of Kerala recognizes Konkani with Devanagari, reinforcing a shift already underway.

catalysts.label: c. 1975
catalysts.text: Kerala Konkani community makes a deliberate, organized decision to use Nagari instead of Malayalam for books and periodicals.
A Kerala meeting urges renewed publishing in Malayalam script, citing UNESCO's endangerment classification and community estimates far above census counts.

scripts.contemporary: Residual but not extinct. The Kudumbi monthly Marg Deepam (Malayalam script) claims 4,000 circulation. A handwritten bi-monthly, The Konkani, was produced in Malayalam script by R. Ranganath Prabhu of Purakkad. The Kerala Konkani Academy has published Malayalam-Konkani reference works. A 2024 survey nonetheless excludes Malayalam from Konkani's currently active scripts. Kerala's 2011 census Konkani total is 69,449.

sources.label: Navhind Times, 'Konkani: the script and the reality'

scripts.name: Perso-Arabic
scripts.subtitle: Nawayathi Konkani
scripts.summary: Nawayathi is Konkani overlaid with Persian, Arabic and Marathi elements, spoken by the Nawayath (Navayat) Muslim community, descended from Goan migrants who intermarried with Arab traders in coastal Karnataka. It was written in Persian/Perso-Arabic script from the outset, comparable in tradition to Arabi-Malayalam and Arwi.

catalysts.label: 16th century
catalysts.text: Goan migrants to coastal Karnataka intermarry with Arab traders, giving rise to the Nawayath community and their Perso-Arabic-influenced Konkani.

catalysts.label: late 17th c.
catalysts.text: Nawayathi begins to be written consistently in Persian/Perso-Arabic script.
Founding of the Anjuman Hami-e-Muslimeen, which chooses Urdu as the community's language of education — relegating Nawayathi to home use only, not taught in schools.
Fortnightly Naqsh-e-Nawayath launched — the principal surviving vehicle for the script, still in print.
A preservation initiative adds three characters to the script and produces a prototype keyboard.

scripts.contemporary: The fortnightly Naqsh-e-Nawayath (founded 1976, relocated to Bhatkal 1996) remains the principal surviving vehicle, printing roughly 3,000 copies of 16 pages per issue. Revival efforts include the Nawayath Mehfil cultural body and the community's first formal dictionary and grammar. Sources disagree sharply: one account holds that Perso-Arabic Konkani publishing ended roughly 50 years ago, while Naqsh-e-Nawayath's continuous run since 1976 directly contradicts that. No official status exists for the script.
